text.p: Following are some of the leading stories in the Swedish papers this morning. Reuters has not verified these stories and does not vouch for their accuracy.

- Swedish Finance Minister Erik Asbrink launches a new attack on the proposed merger between insurer Skandia and mortgage bank Stadshypotek. He said the proposed merger would only benefit a minority of people. Asbrink said the goverment wants to get the best possible price for the state's 34 percent stake in Stadshypotek.

- 1996 has been the worst year ever for flying, even worse than the previous black year, 1985, when 1,800 people died in aeroplane accidents. So far this year an estimated 2,187 people have been killed in plane crashes.

- Car sales have risen strongly this year following a move on taxes on company cars. For the first 11 months of the year 19,147 new cars were registered which was a 26 percent jump on the same period a year ago. BUt the big increase is expected to happen by February next year when companies decide on their new company car strategies.
- A dangerous e-coli bacterial infection in meat, that has affected 75 people across Sweden this year, cannot be traced despite continuing investigations.

- Sweden gets a respite from European Union alcohol rules and will be allowed to continue its present policies over alcohol and tobacco until June 30, 2000. At present the Swedish government has a monopoly over the sale of alcohol in Sweden.

- The Swedish Employers Confederation and the Industry Association has come up with a plan that could create 400,000 new jobs over the new five years. Stopping subsidies to companies worth 30 billion crowns a year and reducing the amount that employers pay for each worker could boost job growth, the two groups said.

- There are strong signals the Swedish economy is improving and will grow at a faster pace over the next few years, fuelled partly by increased private consumption. Swedish GDP is expected to grow by 3.2 percent in 1998 after 1.8 percent growth this year, according to the latest forecast by HUI, the Swedish Retail and Wholesale Research Institute.

- Ericsson and two foreign companies will install broadband networks to enable telecoms operators Telia to provide its residential and small business customers in several cities with high-speed acess to internet and multimedia services.

- Sweden's financial markets are abuzz with speculation about possible new mergers after the recent bid by insurer Skandia for mortgage bank Stadshypotek. One rumour is that S-E-Banken is in talks with Danish bank Unibank.
